name: gnuradio
desc: SDK for signal processing blocks to implement software radios
why: A remarkable software-radio framework, but this formula is deprecated and mostly valuable as a gateway to SDR.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Radio is a free and open-source signal processing runtime and toolkit for building software radios. You build a signal chain from processing blocks, either by writing Python or C++ or by drawing a flowgraph in the GNU Radio Companion GUI. The blocks take in sampled signal data, often from SDR hardware or from files, and output processed signals, sinks, or plots. The README says it is also used to simulate wireless communications. The Homebrew package installs a set of helper executables alongside it, including gnuradio-companion, grcc, gr_modtool, gr_plot, and several uhd_ tools.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says it was originally developed for software-defined radios and for simulating wireless communications, and that its capabilities have led to adoption in hobbyist, academic, and commercial settings. It lists uses ranging from digital communications and radio astronomy to nuclear and particle physics.
brief.how_it_works: Signal processing is organised as blocks wired into flowgraphs, which GNU Radio Companion lets you draw and run. The README says the GUI can run in Qt mode with the --qt flag. The README does not explain the runtime's internal scheduling in detail.

commands_seen.context: Installs GNU Radio from the distribution packages on Debian, Ubuntu, and derivatives. The README says to check your distribution for its version.
Installs the optional Python packages the README lists for dark mode and GUI tests in the Qt version of GNU Radio Companion.
Starts GNU Radio Companion in its Qt interface. The README gives this after the build and install steps.

brief.install_notes: The README recommends the prebuilt packages where they exist, for example sudo apt install gnuradio on Debian and Ubuntu. On Ubuntu, newer builds, both released and from master, are available as PPAs on launchpad.net, and the README warns to uninstall any earlier gnuradio first. Other platforms are covered in the wiki's Quick Start and Other Installation Methods pages. Building from source is described in the wiki's LinuxInstall page. The README no longer recommends PyBOMBS for modern versions. The README does not mention any hardware or account needed to run the core framework. SDR hardware is needed only for live radio work, and the README does not cover it.
brief.standout: The README presents GNU Radio as a runtime and development toolkit rather than just an application. Flowgraphs can be written in Python or built visually and run on the same blocks. A browser version lets people try flowgraphs without installing anything, according to the homepage.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists GNU Radio 4.0.0-RC3 as a news item dated October 13, 2026, and it says RC3 is the first GNU Radio 4 release candidate maintained by the broader community. It also lists a GNU Radio Conference for September 2026 and a European GNU Radio Days event for November 2026. The GitHub README shows a Make Test CI badge. The scout note calls this formula deprecated. That may refer to the Homebrew formula, but I did not find a deprecation notice on the project pages I read.
brief.caveats: The README says GNU Radio 4.0 is in active development in a separate repo, so the Homebrew package may not match the 4.x line. Installation on other platforms points to the wiki and is not covered in the README itself. The README says PyBOMBS is no longer recommended. The bug tracker is for bug reports only and not for usage questions, according to the homepage. The README mentions a COPYING file for licensing but does not state the license in the text I read.
quotes: GNU Radio is a free & open-source signal processing runtime and signal processing software development toolkit.
Originally developed for use with software-defined radios and for simulating wireless communications, it's robust capabilities have led to adoption in hobbyist, academic, and commercial environments.
We are no longer recommending PyBOMBS to install modern versions of GNU Radio.

https://github.com/gnuradio/gnuradio - worked; README returned, used as the main source

judge.reason: GNU Radio turns sampled signals into programmable flowgraphs for building software radios and simulating communications—a substantial, unusual way to explore signal processing.

entry.title: GNU Radio
entry.tldr: A toolkit for building software radios by wiring signal-processing blocks into flowgraphs, drawn in a GUI or written in Python or C++.
entry.deeper_look:
GNU Radio is a free and open-source signal processing runtime and development toolkit. You build a signal chain out of blocks. Each block takes in sampled data, from SDR hardware or from a file, and passes processed data on to the next block, a sink, or a plot. You can assemble the chain in Python or C++, or draw it in GNU Radio Companion and run it from there.

The README says it was originally developed for software-defined radios and for simulating wireless communications. It lists uses in digital communications, radio astronomy, and nuclear and particle physics, across hobbyist, academic, and commercial settings.

The idea underneath is that a radio is a pipeline of mathematical operations on samples: filter, mix, demodulate, decode. Once you see it that way, the hardware is just a source of numbers, and a recorded file works as well as an antenna. That makes it a door into signal processing and radio without needing a bench of equipment.

The Homebrew package installs helper tools alongside the main application, including gnuradio-companion, grcc, gr_modtool, gr_plot, and several uhd_ utilities for Ettus radios.
entry.install:
brew install gnuradio
# Homebrew flags this formula as deprecated. On Debian or Ubuntu the README suggests: sudo apt install gnuradio
# Live radio work needs SDR hardware. Flowgraphs that use files or simulated signals do not.

try_this.what_happens: Opens GNU Radio Companion in its Qt interface, where you drag blocks onto a canvas and connect them into a flowgraph.
Lists the options for the flowgraph editor.
Shows how to plot recorded sample data from a file.

entry.whats_unique: It is a runtime and development toolkit, not just an application. The same blocks can be drawn visually or scripted in Python or C++.
entry.caveats: The Homebrew formula is marked deprecated, and the README says GNU Radio 4.0 is developing in a separate repo, so the brew package may lag the 4.x line.
